focus: Exodus 14 tells how the LORD led Israel to camp by the sea, drew Pharaoh into pursuit, and then saved His people by dividing the waters and overthrowing Egypt’s army. The chapter moves from the LORD’s stated purpose to gain honor over Pharaoh, through Israel’s terror and the commands to stand still and go forward, to the crossing on dry ground and Israel’s fear and faith on the far shore.

sections.title: The LORD Directs Israel to Camp by the Sea
sections.summary: The LORD tells Israel to turn back and camp by the sea before Pi Hahiroth, so that Pharaoh will think the wilderness has closed them in. He will harden Pharaoh’s heart to pursue them and gain honor over him, “that the Egyptians may know that I am the LORD” (Exodus 14:4).

sections.title: Pharaoh Pursues Israel with His Chariots
sections.summary: Pharaoh and his servants regret letting Israel go from serving them, and Pharaoh takes six hundred choice chariots and all the chariots of Egypt. The LORD hardens his heart, and the Egyptian army overtakes Israel camped by the sea, though Israel had gone out with boldness.

sections.title: Israel Cries Out and Moses Calls Them to See the LORD’s Salvation
sections.summary: Seeing the Egyptians, the people cry out to the LORD and accuse Moses of bringing them out to die in the wilderness. Moses answers, “Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD” (Exodus 14:13), and promises, “The LORD will fight for you” (Exodus 14:14).

sections.title: The LORD Commands Israel to Go Forward
sections.summary: The LORD tells Moses, “Tell the children of Israel to go forward” (Exodus 14:15), and commands him to stretch out his rod over the sea and divide it. He will harden the Egyptians’ hearts to follow, and they will know that He is the LORD when He gains honor over Pharaoh’s army.

sections.title: The Angel and the Cloud Protect Israel as the Sea Is Divided
sections.summary: The Angel of God and the pillar of cloud move behind Israel, darkness to Egypt and light to Israel, and the LORD drives back the sea all night so that Israel walks through on dry ground with the waters as a wall on each side. When the Egyptians follow, the LORD troubles their army and takes off their chariot wheels until they cry, “the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians” (Exodus 14:25).

sections.title: The Sea Returns and Israel Fears and Believes the LORD
sections.summary: At the LORD’s command Moses stretches out his hand, the sea returns, and of Pharaoh’s army that followed Israel into the sea “Not so much as one of them remained” (Exodus 14:28). “So the LORD saved Israel that day” (Exodus 14:30), and when Israel sees His great work, they fear the LORD and believe the LORD and His servant Moses.

1.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses with new directions for the journey. The events at the sea begin with God’s own instructions.
1.explain:
“Now the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:”

The events at the sea begin with God’s own word. Every step that follows is under His direction.

2.brief: Israel is to turn back and camp before Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal Zephon. God deliberately places His people where they appear to be trapped.
2.explain:
“Speak to the children of Israel, that they turn and camp before Pi Hahiroth,”

God tells Israel to “turn” back. Instead of pressing on into the wilderness from Etham (13:20), they are to change direction and camp near “Pi Hahiroth.”

“between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal Zephon; you shall camp before it by the sea.”

The camp will be hemmed in: “Migdol” on one side, “the sea” on another, “Baal Zephon” across from them. God deliberately places His people where they appear to be trapped.
2.notes: The exact locations of Pi Hahiroth, Migdol, and Baal Zephon are uncertain. Migdol means tower and may have been an Egyptian fortress. Baal Zephon was the name of a Canaanite god, and the place probably had a shrine to him.

3.brief: Pharaoh will think, “They are bewildered by the land; the wilderness has closed them in.” God’s direction is meant to draw Pharaoh into pursuit.
3.explain:
“For Pharaoh will say of the children of Israel, ‘They are bewildered by the land; the wilderness has closed them in.”

God explains what Pharaoh will think. Israel’s change of direction will look like confusion. “They are bewildered.” To Pharaoh, Israel will seem lost and trapped, an easy target. God’s direction is meant to draw Pharaoh into pursuit.

4.brief: God will harden Pharaoh’s heart to pursue, and He will gain honor over Pharaoh and his army, “that the Egyptians may know that I am the LORD,” and Israel obeys. The coming confrontation will reveal the LORD to Egypt.
4.explain:
“Then I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will pursue them;”

God will “harden Pharaoh’s heart” once more. Pharaoh had let Israel go only under the crushing weight of the last plague. Now God will confirm him in his true desire to get them back.

“and I will gain honor over Pharaoh and over all his army, that the Egyptians may know that I am the LORD.”

God’s purpose is to “gain honor” over Pharaoh and his army. The Hebrew word means to be glorified, to show His weight and greatness. The Egyptians will learn “that I am the LORD.” The coming confrontation will reveal the LORD to Egypt.

“And they did so.”

Israel obeyed. They turned and camped where God told them, though it made no sense by human reasoning.
4.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “gain honor” comes from the root meaning to be heavy, the same root used for Pharaoh’s heart becoming “hard” (heavy) in 7:14; 8:15, 32; 9:7, 34. Pharaoh made his heart heavy against God, and now God will make Himself heavy, that is, glorious, over Pharaoh.

5.brief: When the king of Egypt hears that the people have fled, he and his servants turn against them and ask, “Why have we done this, that we have let Israel go from serving us?” Egypt regrets losing its slaves almost as soon as Israel is gone.
5.explain:
“Now it was told the king of Egypt that the people had fled,”

Word reaches Pharaoh that “the people had fled.” Pharaoh may have expected Israel to return after a three days’ journey to worship (5:3). Their turn toward the sea now looks like flight.

“and the heart of Pharaoh and his servants was turned against the people;”

Pharaoh and his officials change their minds. Their hearts are “turned against the people.” The grief of the last plague gives way to regret.

“and they said, ‘Why have we done this, that we have let Israel go from serving us?”

They ask “Why have we done this?” Their concern is the loss of their labor force. Israel had been serving Egypt. Egypt regrets losing its slaves almost as soon as Israel is gone.

6.brief: Pharaoh makes his chariot ready and takes his people with him. The king himself leads the pursuit.
6.explain:
“So he made ready his chariot and took his people with him.”

Pharaoh himself prepares “his chariot.” The king leads the pursuit in person, with his troops.

7.brief: Pharaoh takes six hundred choice chariots and all the chariots of Egypt, with captains over every one of them. Egypt’s chariot force pursues Israel in full strength.
7.explain:
“Also, he took six hundred choice chariots,”

Pharaoh brings “six hundred choice chariots,” his elite force.

“and all the chariots of Egypt with captains over every one of them.”

He adds “all the chariots of Egypt,” each under an officer. Egypt sends its full chariot strength. Chariots were the most powerful weapon of the age, and Israel had none.
7.notes: The Hebrew word translated “captains” may refer to the third man in a chariot or to officers of high rank. Its exact sense is debated.

8.brief: The LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he pursues the children of Israel, who had gone out with boldness. Pharaoh’s pursuit fulfills what God said, while Israel had left confidently.
8.explain:
“And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the children of Israel;”

What God said in 14:4 now happens. “The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh,” and Pharaoh sets out after Israel.

“and the children of Israel went out with boldness.”

Israel had left Egypt “with boldness,” literally with a high hand. They went out openly and confidently, not as runaways sneaking away. Pharaoh’s pursuit fulfills what God said, while Israel had left with confidence.
8.notes: The phrase “with boldness” reads literally with a high hand. Numbers 33:3 uses the same expression of Israel leaving Egypt “in the sight of all the Egyptians.”

9.brief: The Egyptian army, with all Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, horsemen, and soldiers, overtakes Israel camped by the sea near Pi Hahiroth. Israel is caught between the army and the water.
9.explain:
“So the Egyptians pursued them, all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, his horsemen and his army,”

The whole force of Egypt pursues: horses, chariots, horsemen, and army.

“and overtook them camping by the sea beside Pi Hahiroth, before Baal Zephon.”

They catch up with Israel at the very place God had told them to camp (14:2). Israel is caught between the army and the water.

10.brief: When Israel sees the Egyptians marching after them, they are very afraid and cry out to the LORD. Their boldness turns to fear at the sight of Pharaoh’s army.
10.explain:
“And when Pharaoh drew near, the children of Israel lifted their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians marched after them.”

Israel looks up and sees “the Egyptians marched after them.” The army they thought they had escaped is coming.

“So they were very afraid, and the children of Israel cried out to the LORD.”

Israel’s boldness (14:8) turns to fear. They are “very afraid.” They do the right thing in crying “out to the LORD.” But what they say next shows how deep their fear runs.

11.brief: The people ask Moses, “Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness?” Their fear turns into bitter accusation against Moses.
11.explain:
“Then they said to Moses, ‘Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness?”

The people turn on Moses with bitter sarcasm. Egypt was famous for its tombs and burial places. “Because there were no graves in Egypt” mocks the idea that Moses had to bring them out to die. Their fear turns into accusation.

“Why have you so dealt with us, to bring us up out of Egypt?”

They blame Moses for the exodus itself. They speak as though Moses, not God, had brought them out.

12.brief: The people remind Moses that they had told him in Egypt to leave them alone, saying it would be better to serve the Egyptians than die in the wilderness. In their panic they prefer slavery to trusting God.
12.explain:
“Is this not the word that we told you in Egypt, saying, ‘Let us alone that we may serve the Egyptians’?”

The people claim they had warned Moses in Egypt. The text earlier records the foremen complaining after Pharaoh increased their burdens (5:20–21) and the people not heeding Moses (6:9).

“For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than that we should die in the wilderness.”

Their conclusion is that slavery would have been “better” than dying in the wilderness. In their panic they prefer slavery to trusting God. This complaint will return again and again in the wilderness (16:3; 17:3; Numbers 14:2–4).

13.brief: Moses answers, “Do not be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD,” and promises that they will never again see these Egyptians. Moses calls the people to trust God and watch Him act.
13.explain:
“And Moses said to the people, ‘Do not be afraid.”

Moses answers their fear with God’s word. “Do not be afraid.”

“Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which He will accomplish for you today.”

Moses calls them to “stand still,” to stand firm and hold their ground rather than flee or fight. They are to “see the salvation of the LORD.” The deliverance will be God’s work, done “for you today.”

“For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall see again no more forever.”

Moses promises that the enemy they fear will be gone for good. The Egyptians they see “today” they will “see again no more forever.”
13.notes: This is the first use of the Hebrew word for “salvation” (yeshuah) in Exodus. It comes from the same root as the name Joshua and the name Jesus (Matthew 1:21).

14.brief: “The LORD will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace.” The battle belongs to the LORD, and the people’s part is to trust Him quietly.
14.explain:
“The LORD will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace.”

The battle belongs to the LORD. “The LORD will fight for you.” Israel’s part is to “hold your peace,” to be still and quiet, trusting Him. They will not have to raise a weapon. Moses calls them to quiet trust in the LORD who fights for them.
14.notes: The same assurance appears in Deuteronomy 1:30 and 3:22, and in Jehoshaphat’s day, “the battle is not yours, but God’s” (2 Chronicles 20:15).

15.brief: The LORD says to Moses, “Why do you cry to Me? Tell the children of Israel to go forward.” The call to stand and see is followed by the command to move.
15.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Why do you cry to Me?”

God speaks to Moses. “Why do you cry to Me?” The text has not recorded Moses crying out, but he may have been praying along with the people (14:10). Now is not the time to keep calling out. It is time to act.

“Tell the children of Israel to go forward.”

God commands Israel to “go forward.” Moses had told them to stand still and see God’s salvation (14:13). Now God tells them to move. Standing still meant not giving in to panic. Going forward meant obeying when God opened the way. Both belong together. They stand firm in trust, and they move when God speaks.

16.brief: Moses is to lift up his rod and stretch his hand over the sea and divide it, so that Israel can go through on dry ground. God opens the way for His people to obey.
16.explain:
“But lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it.”

God tells Moses what to do. He is to “lift up your rod” and “stretch out your hand over the sea.” The rod that brought the plagues will now open the sea. Moses acts, but it is God who will “divide it.”

“And the children of Israel shall go on dry ground through the midst of the sea.”

Israel will walk “on dry ground” through the middle of the sea. God opens the way so that His people can obey.

17.brief: God will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they follow, and He will gain honor over Pharaoh, his army, chariots, and horsemen. Egypt’s pursuit into the sea will become the place of God’s victory.
17.explain:
“And I indeed will harden the hearts of the Egyptians, and they shall follow them.”

God will “harden the hearts of the Egyptians” so that they follow Israel into the sea. The hardening that began with Pharaoh now extends to his army.

“So I will gain honor over Pharaoh and over all his army, his chariots, and his horsemen.”

God will “gain honor” over every part of Egypt’s force. Egypt’s pursuit into the sea will become the place of God’s victory.

18.brief: “Then the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD,” when God has gained honor over Pharaoh’s forces. The purpose stated in verse 4 is repeated.
18.explain:
“Then the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD,”

The purpose stated in 14:4 is repeated. The Egyptians will “know that I am the LORD.” Pharaoh asked, “Who is the LORD?” (5:2). The sea will give the final answer.

“when I have gained honor for Myself over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.”

The knowledge will come through God’s victory. When God has shown His glory over Pharaoh’s forces, Egypt will know who He is.

19.brief: The Angel of God, who went before Israel, moves behind them, and the pillar of cloud moves from the front to stand behind them. God places His own presence between His people and their enemies, and this Angel, like the Angel at the bush, is likely an appearance of Christ.
19.explain:
“And the Angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them;”

“The Angel of God,” who had been leading Israel, moves to the rear. He places Himself between Israel and the army. This Angel, like the Angel of the LORD at the burning bush (3:2–6), is likely an appearance of Christ before His incarnation.

“and the pillar of cloud went from before them and stood behind them.”

The pillar of cloud moves with Him, from the front to the back of the camp. God’s presence that guided them now guards them. God places His own presence between His people and their enemies.
19.notes: In 13:21 it is the LORD who goes before Israel in the pillar. Here it is the Angel of God who moves to the rear along with the pillar.

20.brief: The cloud comes between the camps, darkness to Egypt and light to Israel by night, so that neither comes near the other all night. The same presence that protects Israel hides them from Egypt.
20.explain:
“So it came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel.”

The cloud stands “between” the two camps. It forms a barrier the Egyptians cannot pass.

“Thus it was a cloud and darkness to the one, and it gave light by night to the other,”

The same cloud has two effects. To Egypt it is “a cloud and darkness.” To Israel it gives “light by night.” As in the ninth plague (10:22–23), God makes a distinction between His people and Egypt.

“so that the one did not come near the other all that night.”

All night long the Egyptians cannot reach Israel. The same presence that protects Israel hides them from Egypt.

21.brief: Moses stretches out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drives the sea back by a strong east wind all night, making dry land as the waters are divided. The LORD Himself opens the way through the sea.
21.explain:
“Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea;”

Moses obeys the command of 14:16.

“and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea into dry land, and the waters were divided.”

The sea did not part by chance. God used “a strong east wind” that blew “all that night,” but the wind was His instrument. The sea became “dry land,” and the “waters were divided.” The LORD Himself opens the way through the sea.
21.notes: The song in 15:8 describes the same event poetically, saying the waters were gathered together “with the blast of Your nostrils.” The wind is God’s breath.

22.brief: The children of Israel go into the midst of the sea on dry ground, with the waters as a wall on their right and left. Israel walks to safety through the path God has made.
22.explain:
“So the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground,”

Israel walks “into the midst of the sea.” They go forward as God commanded, on “dry ground.”

“and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.”

The water stands “a wall” on both sides. This is no ordinary low tide. Israel walks between walls of water. Israel walks to safety through the path God has made.
22.notes: Hebrews 11:29 says, “By faith they passed through the Red Sea as by dry land, whereas the Egyptians, attempting to do so, were drowned.”

23.brief: The Egyptians pursue them into the midst of the sea with all Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen. Egypt’s army follows Israel into the path God opened.
23.explain:
“And the Egyptians pursued and went after them into the midst of the sea,”

The Egyptians follow Israel “into the midst of the sea.” Their hardened hearts drive them on (14:17).

“all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.”

The whole of Pharaoh’s mounted force enters the path God opened for Israel.

24.brief: In the morning watch the LORD looks down on the Egyptian army through the pillar of fire and cloud and throws them into confusion. The LORD now acts directly against the pursuing army.
24.explain:
“Now it came to pass, in the morning watch,”

“The morning watch” was the last part of the night, before dawn.

“that the LORD looked down upon the army of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, and He troubled the army of the Egyptians.”

God watches the army from the pillar, and His look alone brings judgment. He “troubled” them, throwing them into panic and confusion. The LORD now acts directly against the pursuing army.
24.notes:
The night was divided into three watches in Old Testament times (Judges 7:19; Lamentations 2:19). The morning watch was roughly from 2 to 6 a.m.

Psalm 77:16–19 describes thunder, lightning, and rain at the sea, which may have been part of the confusion God sent.

25.brief: God takes off their chariot wheels so that they drive with difficulty, and the Egyptians cry, “the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians.” Egypt itself confesses what Moses promised in verse 14.
25.explain:
“And He took off their chariot wheels, so that they drove them with difficulty;”

God “took off their chariot wheels,” or caused them to swerve or clog. The chariots, Egypt’s pride, now bog down and drag.

“and the Egyptians said, ‘Let us flee from the face of Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians.”

At last the Egyptians recognize the truth. What Moses promised in 14:14 the enemy now confesses. They try to flee, but it is too late.
25.notes: The Greek and Samaritan texts read He bound their chariot wheels, suggesting that the wheels became stuck.

26.brief: The LORD tells Moses to stretch out his hand over the sea so that the waters return on the Egyptians, their chariots, and horsemen. The same hand that divided the sea will bring it back.
26.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the waters may come back upon the Egyptians, on their chariots, and on their horsemen.”

God commands Moses to stretch out his hand once more. The hand that divided the sea will bring it back. The “waters” will return “upon the Egyptians.”

27.brief: Moses stretches out his hand, and at daybreak the sea returns to its full depth while the Egyptians are fleeing into it, “So the LORD overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea.” The LORD is the One who defeats Egypt.
27.explain:
“And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and when the morning appeared, the sea returned to its full depth,”

At daybreak, “the sea returned to its full depth,” its normal flow.

“while the Egyptians were fleeing into it.”

The Egyptians, trying to escape, run straight into the returning waters.

“So the LORD overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea.”

The narrator makes clear who did this. The word “overthrew” means to shake off or toss. God threw the army into the sea. The LORD is the One who defeats Egypt.
27.notes: The song in 15:1, 4, 21 celebrates this moment: “The horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea!”

28.brief: The waters return and cover the chariots, horsemen, and all of Pharaoh’s army that entered the sea, “Not so much as one of them remained.” The army that pursued Israel into the sea is completely destroyed.
28.explain:
“Then the waters returned and covered the chariots, the horsemen, and all the army of Pharaoh that came into the sea after them.”

The waters “covered” the whole army that entered the sea.

“Not so much as one of them remained.”

The destruction was total. No one from the force that followed Israel into the sea survived. Moses’ promise was fulfilled: Israel would not see these Egyptians again (14:13).
28.notes: The text does not say whether Pharaoh himself entered the sea and died. Psalm 136:15 says God “overthrew Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea,” which may describe the defeat of his power rather than his personal death.

29.brief: But the children of Israel had walked on dry land through the sea, with the waters as a wall on both sides. The narrator sets Israel’s safe passage beside Egypt’s destruction.
29.explain:
“But the children of Israel had walked on dry land in the midst of the sea,”

The narrator sets Israel’s experience beside Egypt’s. While Egypt drowned, Israel “had walked on dry land.”

“and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.”

The same waters that were “a wall” of protection for Israel became a flood of judgment for Egypt. The narrator sets Israel’s safe passage beside Egypt’s destruction.

30.brief: “So the LORD saved Israel that day out of the hand of the Egyptians,” and Israel sees the Egyptians dead on the seashore. The deliverance is complete and visible.
30.explain:
“So the LORD saved Israel that day out of the hand of the Egyptians,”

The verse sums up the event. “The LORD saved Israel.” The salvation Moses promised (14:13) has come “that day.”

“and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.”

Israel “saw the Egyptians dead” on the shore. The deliverance was complete and visible. The enemy that had pursued them was gone.

31.brief: Israel sees the great work the LORD has done, “so the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD and His servant Moses.” The sight of God’s salvation leads His people to reverence and faith.
31.explain:
“Thus Israel saw the great work which the LORD had done in Egypt;”

Israel “saw the great work,” literally the great hand, of the LORD. The phrase recalls the strong hand by which God brought them out (13:3, 9, 14, 16).

“so the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD and His servant Moses.”

The sight of God’s salvation changes Israel’s response. The people who were very afraid of the Egyptians (14:10) now “feared the LORD.” Their fear turns to reverence. They “believed the LORD and His servant Moses.” The people who accused Moses (14:11–12) now trust him as God’s servant. The sight of God’s salvation leads His people to reverence and faith. Paul later describes Israel as having been “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2).
